source_coverage: AP Biology Unit 3 (Cellular Energetics) photosynthesis lecture slides 12-34: light reactions, chemiosmosis, Calvin cycle, photorespiration, C4/CAM, limiting factors.

concepts.name: Light absorption by pigments
concepts.summary: Chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b and carotenoids in thylakoid membranes absorb specific wavelengths; absorbed energy is funneled to reaction-center chlorophyll.
facts: Chlorophyll a absorbs blue-violet and red light best and reflects green.
Accessory pigments pass energy to the reaction center.
P680 (PSII) and P700 (PSI) are named for their absorption peaks.
An action spectrum tracks the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll.

misconceptions.wrong: Plants look green because they absorb green light the most.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Green is the color least absorbed; it is reflected or transmitted, which is why we see it.

concepts.name: Photolysis (water splitting)
concepts.summary: Photosystem II splits water to replace its lost electrons, releasing O2 and H+ into the thylakoid lumen.
facts: All O2 released by photosynthesis comes from water (18O tracer experiments).
H+ from water adds to the lumen gradient.

misconceptions.wrong: The oxygen released by plants comes from carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Isotope tracer experiments show labeled O in water, not CO2, appears in the O2; CO2's oxygen ends up in sugar and water.

concepts.name: Linear electron flow
concepts.summary: Electrons move from PSII through plastoquinone, the cytochrome b6f complex and plastocyanin to PSI, then to NADP+ reductase, making NADPH; cyclic flow around PSI makes ATP only.
facts: Electron flow is PSII -> Pq -> cytochrome complex -> Pc -> PSI -> Fd -> NADP+ reductase.
The cytochrome complex pumps H+ into the lumen.
Herbicide DCMU blocks electron transfer from PSII to plastoquinone, stopping O2 release and NADPH production.
Cyclic electron flow makes ATP but no NADPH or O2.
steps: PSII absorbs light and loses an electron
Plastoquinone carries it to the cytochrome complex

misconceptions.wrong: Light energy is used directly to make glucose.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Light energy is converted to ATP and NADPH first; the Calvin cycle uses those to make sugar.

concepts.name: Chemiosmosis in the chloroplast
concepts.summary: An H+ gradient (high in the lumen, low in the stroma) drives H+ through ATP synthase into the stroma, making ATP.
facts: Lumen pH ~5, stroma pH ~8 in bright light.
Each pH unit is a 10-fold difference in H+ concentration.
ATP is made on the stroma side, where the Calvin cycle uses it.
Uncouplers that make the membrane leaky stop ATP synthesis but not electron flow.

misconceptions.wrong: H+ flows from the stroma into the lumen to make ATP.
misconceptions.why_wrong: H+ is pumped INTO the lumen; ATP synthase is driven as H+ flows back OUT to the stroma, down its gradient.

concepts.name: Calvin cycle
concepts.summary: In the stroma, Rubisco fixes CO2 onto RuBP; ATP and NADPH reduce 3-PGA to G3P; most G3P regenerates RuBP.
facts: 3 CO2 -> 1 net G3P, costing 9 ATP and 6 NADPH.
Each CO2 fixed costs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
Phases: fixation, reduction, regeneration.
The cycle depends on light-reaction products, so it runs in daylight.

formulas.expr: ATP = 3 * CO2; NADPH = 2 * CO2; G3P_net = CO2 / 3

steps: Fixation: Rubisco attaches CO2 to RuBP
Reduction: ATP and NADPH convert 3-PGA to G3P
Regeneration: G3P rebuilt into RuBP using ATP

misconceptions.wrong: The Calvin cycle ('dark reactions') happens at night.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions and light-activated enzymes, so it runs during the day.

misconceptions.wrong: Plants get most of their mass from the soil.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The carbon in plant biomass comes from CO2 fixed by the Calvin cycle.

concepts.name: Rubisco and photorespiration
concepts.summary: Rubisco can bind O2 instead of CO2; photorespiration consumes ATP and releases CO2 without making sugar, worse when hot and when stomata are closed.
facts: High O2:CO2 ratio and high temperature favor oxygenation.
Photorespiration wastes fixed carbon and ATP.
Closed stomata let O2 build up and CO2 fall inside the leaf.

misconceptions.wrong: Photorespiration is the same as cellular respiration and produces ATP.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Photorespiration consumes ATP and releases CO2 without producing ATP or sugar.

concepts.name: C4 and CAM adaptations
concepts.summary: C4 plants fix CO2 with PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells and deliver it to Rubisco in bundle-sheath cells (spatial separation); CAM plants fix CO2 at night and use it by day (temporal separation).
facts: PEP carboxylase has no affinity for O2.
In C4 plants the Calvin cycle runs in bundle-sheath cells.
CAM plants open stomata at night.
C4 costs extra ATP, which pays off in hot climates.

misconceptions.wrong: In C4 plants Rubisco works in the mesophyll cells alongside PEP carboxylase.
misconceptions.why_wrong: C4 separates the steps in space: PEP carboxylase in mesophyll, Rubisco in bundle-sheath cells where CO2 is concentrated.

concepts.name: Limiting factors
concepts.summary: The photosynthesis rate is set by whichever input is in shortest supply: light intensity, CO2 concentration, or temperature; the Calvin cycle is limited by whichever of ATP or NADPH runs out first.
facts: At low light, adding CO2 barely helps.
Above an optimum temperature, enzymes denature and the rate falls.
Linear electron flow supplies slightly too little ATP relative to NADPH; cyclic flow makes up the difference.

variables.CO2_fixed: CO2 the Calvin cycle can fix

misconceptions.wrong: Increasing any one input always increases the rate of photosynthesis.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Only increasing the limiting input raises the rate; the others are already in excess.
